items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that we have a straight line passing through the point [MATH: P(3,-1,7)] and that's parallel to the direction vector [MATH: [0; 5; − 3]] As we know, we can write the vector equation of the line as follows:

Content:
[MATH: r|= p + tv; r|= [3; − 1; 7] + t[0; 5; − 3],]
where [MATH: t \in (-\infty,\infty).]

Content:
Using the vector equation above, we can create a set of parametric equations where we express a general point [MATH: (x,y,z)] in terms of the parameter [MATH: t.]

Content:
If we let [MATH: [x; y; z]] be the position vector of the general point [MATH: (x,y,z),] then the above equation can be written as

Content:
[MATH: r|= [3; − 1; 7] + t[0; 5; − 3]; [x; y; z]|= [3; − 1; 7] + t[0; 5; − 3]; [x; y; z]|= [3; − 1 + 5t; 7 − 3t].]

Content:
So, we have the following system of equations:
[MATH: x = 3; y = − 1 + 5t; z = 7 − 3t]

Content:
The equations in the above system are called the parametric equations of the straight line.
Geometrically, the equation states that a point belongs to the line if and only if its coordinates have the form

Content:
[MATH: (3, \: -1+5t, \: 7-3t),]

Content:
where [MATH: t \in (-\infty, \infty).]

[MATH: r|= p + tv; r|= [1; − 5; 3] + t[− 1; 9; − 7]; [x; y; z]|= [1; − 5; 3] + [− t; 9t; − 7t]; [x; y; z]|= [1 − t; − 5 + 9t; 3 − 7t]]

where [MATH: t \in (-\infty,\infty).]

Therefore, the parametric equations of the line segment [MATH: \overline{PQ}] are the following: [MATH: {x = 1 − t; y = − 5 + 9t; z = 3 − 7t]
